name: bluewater-shorts-73-82
lines: It's eleven p.m. You're still working.
But look at what you're working on.
A quote. An invoice. A post that four people saw.
A missed call from six o'clock, that you only just noticed.
You're the best in town at one thing.
And at night, you're a beginner at five others.
Nobody told you the trade was the easy part.
You were never supposed to do all of this alone.
Your business. Our marketing department.
Sailors have a name for the open sea.
The part with no land in sight. No harbor. Nobody to follow.
They call it blue water.
It's where every business owner works.
No boss. No map. No one to ask if you're doing it right.
Just you, deciding. Every single day.
Most people never leave the harbor. You did.
So if you're out there tonight, here's what we want you to know.
You don't have to sail it alone.
Our real numbers. And the part agencies hide.
One client. Forty four inbound calls, recorded from January first to February sixteenth, twenty twenty six.
Four hundred seventy dollars and ninety five cents in Google ad spend, from January fourteenth to February fourteenth.
Four thousand, five hundred sixty one impressions in that ad period.
Now the fine print. We read it out loud.
Those two date ranges don't match.
And these records don't prove every call came from the ads. Or that every call became a booked job.
Most marketing leaves that part out. We put it on our website.
If a number can't survive its own fine print, it's not a result. It's a sales pitch.
You're in your customer's phone. Under a name you didn't pick.
Let's scroll one. Made up phone. Real habit.
Dave, fence guy. Do not answer.
A C guy. Expensive.
Plumber. The one who actually came.
Maria, electrician. Gold star. Use her for everything.
Nobody saves your logo. Or your slogan.
They save how it felt to deal with you.
That's your brand. It's what they call you when you're not in the room.
Three reasons not to hire us.
One. You want a guarantee. Page one. Fifty leads. A number by a date.
We won't give you one. Nobody honest can.
Two. You need it to work by Friday.
Real marketing is slow at the start. Month one is mostly work you can't see.
Three. You only want the good news.
We show you what worked. And what flopped. On the same page.
Still here? Then we should probably talk.
Nobody's going to say this to you. So we will.
Nobody claps when you make payroll.
Nobody saw you redo that job for free, because it wasn't right.
Nobody counts the birthdays you were late to.
You answer the phone on vacation. You know your customers' dogs by name.
And every month, people get paid because you didn't quit.
That's not a small business. That's a big deal.
We see it. We built this company for people like you.
We put marketing promises on a lie detector.
Promise one. We'll get you to the top of Google in thirty days.
Lie. Nobody controls the top spot. Google says so itself.
Promise two. Guaranteed leads, or your money back.
Half true. Read the small print. A lead can be anyone. Even a wrong number.
Promise three. You'll see every dollar, and what it did.
True. Boring. And weirdly rare.
The truth never sounds as good as the pitch. Pick it anyway.
Here we see the contractor, attempting marketing.
It is nine p.m. He has not eaten.
He opens the app. He stares. He closes the app.
A bold move. He posts a blurry photo of a water heater. No caption.
Two likes. One is his mother.
Exhausted, he returns to what he is actually good at.
In the wild, this cycle repeats every three months.
He doesn't need motivation. He needs a department.
Marketing is an iceberg. You're only seeing the tip.
One post. One ad. One new photo. That's the part above the water.
Now look underneath.
A listing, corrected. A website, rewritten so a stranger gets it in five seconds.
Tracking, so every call has a source.
Reviews, asked for the right way. Follow up, written before anyone needs it.
Like any iceberg, most of it sits below the line.
So if month one feels quiet, it isn't. It's underwater.
This ad is around a thousand years old.
It's one of the oldest printed ads we know of. For a needle shop, in Song dynasty China.
And it does four things most businesses still don't.
One. A name. Liu's Fine Needle Shop. You know exactly what they sell.
Two. A logo. A white rabbit.
Three. A promise. Good steel, fine needles, ready fast.
Four. Where to find them. Look for the rabbit at the door.
A name. A mark. A promise. A way in.
A thousand years later, that's still the whole job.
